questions.stem: In the ED, you examine Farihah, 34, who has sharp pleuritic chest pain that eases when she sits forward. With her sitting forward, you hear a scratchy, superficial sound at the left lower sternal edge. Which manoeuvre best tells you whether this is a pericardial rub rather than a pleural rub?
options: Ask her to cough, then listen again for any change in the sound
Ask her to hold her breath and listen for whether the sound persists
Roll her into the left lateral position and listen at the apex with the bell
Ask her to perform a Valsalva manoeuvre and listen during the strain
questions.why: A pleural rub depends on the pleural layers sliding over each other, so it stops when breathing stops. A pericardial rub comes from the heart moving, so it carries on when she holds her breath. Listen with the diaphragm, with her sitting forward in held expiration.
notes: Coughing tells you whether crackles are from secretions. It does not separate a pericardial rub from a pleural rub.
The left lateral position with the bell is for low-pitched mitral murmurs. Lying back also makes her pain worse, and a rub is heard best with her sitting forward.
Valsalva is used to bring out the dynamic murmurs of HOCM and mitral valve prolapse. It does not show whether a rub depends on breathing.

questions.stem: Farihah, 34, weighs 64 kg and has acute pericarditis. Her troponins are normal, she has no high-risk features and she is for discharge. You have charted ibuprofen 600 mg orally 8-hourly with a proton pump inhibitor. Which colchicine regimen is most appropriate to add?
options: Colchicine 500 micrograms orally once daily for 3 months
Colchicine 500 micrograms orally twice daily for 3 months
Colchicine 1 mg orally, then 500 micrograms 1 hour later, once only
Colchicine 500 micrograms orally once daily for 2 weeks
questions.why: For a first episode of acute pericarditis, colchicine is dosed by weight: 500 micrograms once daily under 70 kg, or twice daily from 70 kg. It is given for 3 months alongside the NSAID and roughly halves the risk of recurrence.
notes: Twice-daily dosing is for patients weighing 70 kg or more. At 64 kg she should take it once daily.
This is the short loading regimen for acute gout. It is not the pericarditis regimen and gives no protection against recurrence.
Two weeks is roughly how long the NSAID runs. Colchicine is continued for 3 months to reduce recurrence.

questions.stem: Farihah, 34, has acute pericarditis. Her ECG shows widespread concave ST elevation, PR segment depression in II, aVF, V2 and V3, and PR elevation in aVR. Her PR interval is 150 ms and her QRS is 86 ms. What best explains the PR segment depression?
options: Slowed conduction through the AV node, prolonging the PR segment beyond normal limits
Increased vagal tone from pain slowing atrial depolarisation
Early ventricular depolarisation through an accessory pathway
Atrial epicardial inflammation producing an atrial current of injury
questions.why: The inflammation also involves the epicardium over the atria. This produces an atrial current of injury that shifts the PR segment away from baseline: depressed in most leads and elevated in aVR. It is the atrial counterpart of the ventricular ST elevation.
notes: AV nodal delay makes the PR interval longer but leaves the segment on the baseline. Her PR interval is a normal 150 ms.
She is tachycardic, which goes against high vagal tone. Vagal tone would change the rate or the PR interval, not move the PR segment off baseline.
Pre-excitation gives a short PR interval with a delta wave and a broad QRS. Her PR is 150 ms and her QRS is a narrow 86 ms.

questions.stem: Farihah, 34, has sharp retrosternal pain from acute pericarditis. She says she has also felt it in her neck. Which nerve carries pain from the inflamed parietal pericardium and best explains why she feels it in her neck?
options: Vagus nerve, via its cardiac branches
Upper thoracic intercostal nerves (T1 to T4)
Phrenic nerve, from the C3 to C5 roots
Cardiac sympathetic afferents to T1 to T4
questions.why: The parietal pericardium is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5), so its pain is referred to the C3 to C5 dermatomes of the neck, shoulder and trapezius ridge. The visceral pericardium is largely insensitive to pain.
notes: The vagus carries visceral afferents for cardiac reflexes, not well-localised pericardial pain that is referred to the neck.
The intercostal nerves supply the chest wall and costal pleura. Pain carried by them would be referred along thoracic dermatomes, not to the neck.
Cardiac sympathetic afferents carry ischaemic pain from the myocardium, not pain from the parietal pericardium, which is carried by the phrenic nerve.
